title: Love all creation
hookLine: Dostoevsky's Zosima: love every leaf, every ray of light, the animals, the plants
tomorrow: what if you're too small for the stairs everyone else climbs?

lines: A WEED, A SPIDER, A STRANGER'S DOG.
cards: A weed pushing out of a sidewalk crack. A spider in the corner of the shower. A dog that isn't yours, waiting outside a store.
How small can a thing be and still be worth loving? In a long Russian novel, an old monk answers by naming things that small. Love all God's creation, he says, every grain of sand.
Love every leaf, every ray of God's light. Love the animals, love the plants, love everything.

teach.h: ZOSIMA, A MONK IN A NOVEL.
teach.b: The monk is Father Zosima, in Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov. He's a novelist's character, so the novel itself is the source.
His reason is the surprise: love everything, and you'll begin to perceive God's mystery in things.

teach.h: VERY GOOD, ONE LEAF AT A TIME.
teach.b: Underneath is the first page of the Bible, in Genesis: “God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good.” Zosima's love agrees with that verdict, one leaf at a time. Not nature as an idea.
A single leaf, with a torn edge and a stem.
Now hold the whole week up to the light. A spiritual's question at the cross, answered with trembling. A deep river, and home gathered on the far side.
A pilgrim asking how to pray always, and a prayer that learned to pray itself. A poet with empty hands who gave her heart. A worn world, charged with grandeur.
And today, every leaf. Songs, a pilgrim, two poets and a novelist, each pointing past its own page.

how: Some Christians pray blessings over animals, fields and gardens, and some read Zosima's words as a guide for living gently with creation.

o: a feast day blessing the fields at harvest time
Zosima's call to love every part of what God made
a vow monks take to live only off the land

games.q: the week's voices — tap the pairs.
p: an old monk in a novel

s: Zosima is a historical Russian saint
he's a character in Dostoevsky's novel; the novel is the source.
loving creation means loving nature instead of God
Zosima loves it as God's creation, and Genesis calls it very good.
in Zosima's teaching, love comes before the seeing
love everything, and you'll begin to perceive God's mystery in things.

games.q: your little sister wants to stomp an ant hill "because they're just bugs." which sentence fits Zosima's teaching?
o: "they're tiny, but they're part of what God made. let's watch them instead."
"leave them alone, or they'll bite you and it'll hurt."
"only people matter to God, but stomping is still kind of mean."
games.why: Zosima says love every leaf, the animals, everything, as God's creation. Genesis calls all of it very good.

practice: If there's a plant, a leaf or a flower within reach, hold it, or bring your face close and breathe in its smell. Find one detail you'd never notice in passing: a vein, a torn edge, a speck of dust.
Stay with that one living thing for the whole sit, as if it were the only one.

wordCard.voice: Love all creation. Zosima's teaching in Dostoevsky's novel: love every part of what God made, down to the leaf.

orig.note: Hebrew for 'very good' in Genesis 1:31, the verdict Zosima's love agrees with.

carryVoice: The line for this week's end: love every leaf. Not nature in general; one leaf, with a torn edge. Seven days, done.
